name: multiple-views
intent: Keep one presentation-free model behind several independent view technologies, so each representation is produced by its own view while the domain data, its derivation rules and its consistency stay in one place.
problem: A single body of data must be published through more than one presentation technology at the same time - an HTML page, a JSON or XML API, a CSV or PDF export, a mobile channel. Each technology is easy to satisfy with its own copy of the loading, filtering and formatting logic, so the representations drift apart and every model change has to be repeated per technology.
context: Server-side presentation layers of enterprise applications (and document/GUI tools) where one model is read by several rendering technologies, whether concurrently (a page and an API over the same resource; a table and a chart over the same document) or over time (channels added later), and where the model must stay unaware of any particular presentation technology.
benefits: One home for the domain data and its derivation rules: the model is loaded, validated and transformed once, and every representation reads the same values instead of its own copy of the business rules.
New representations are additive: a new view technology (PDF export, mobile channel, feed, partner XML) is a new view plus a registration, not a change to the model or to the existing views.

Cross-channel consistency: because all views share the model - and, where extracted, the same logical view or presentation model - field selection, rounding, locale and date rules cannot silently diverge.
Each technology is used idiomatically: markup stays in templates, payloads in serializers, documents in writers, instead of one technology being bent to serve every channel.
Views are independently testable and independently cacheable: each can be exercised against a fixed model, and expensive representations can be cached (Page Cache) without caching the model itself.
The model can evolve and be reused: keeping it presentation-free lets the same data surface through a rich client, a report and an API without leaking presentation choices into the domain.
tradeoffs: Presentation logic is multiplied: unless a shared presentation model or logical view is extracted, each view repeats field selection and formatting, and the copies drift as the model changes.
Every model change touches every representation and every representation's tests; the maintenance surface grows with the number of view technologies, not with the amount of data.
Serialization leaks are easy: handing the domain object straight to a serializer exposes internals the HTML view never showed, and can fire lazy loading or expose relations per element.

The selection indirection hides decisions: negotiation edge cases (browsers sending */*, unparsable or unsupported media types, 406 versus silent fallback, URL-suffix heuristics) make the rendered representation surprising far from the handler that built the model.

Cost is spread and uneven: per-request rendering and serialization differ per representation, and view-resolver ordering, engine registration and formatter registration become deployment-critical configuration.
Debugging spans more layers: a wrong page may originate in the model, the chosen view, the negotiation configuration, or a per-format escaping difference that only one representation triggers.

participants.responsibility: Holds the presentation-agnostic data and behaviour that every view reads; it is aware of neither the views nor their technologies and exposes the same values to all of them.
Renders the model in exactly one technology or format (HTML template, JSON serializer, XML transform, CSV or PDF writer, live widget) and can be produced without the other views.
Decides which view serves a request from the requested representation (Accept header, media type, format suffix, channel) and is the single place where 'which view technology?' is answered.
Carries technology-independent presentation state shared by the views, so field selection and formatting rules are written once instead of once per representation.
Notifies or invalidates the attached views when the model changes; needed only when several views stay alive at the same time, unnecessary for on-demand rendering.
Obtains the model, reshapes it into the shared projection and hands it to the negotiation point; it never formats the data itself.

use_cases: A resource served both as an HTML page and as a JSON API from one model and one set of business rules (server-side rendering beside an API in the same application).
Exports beside the UI: the same dataset as HTML, CSV and PDF for reporting, with filtering and selection rules defined once.
Multi-channel delivery: web pages, mobile screens, feeds and partner XML from one model, with channel-specific markup over shared content.
A desktop or tool application with several simultaneous presentations of one document (table, chart, inspector) that must stay synchronized while editing.
Migration periods where an old and a new presentation technology (JSP beside Thymeleaf, XML beside JSON) are served from the same model until every consumer has moved.
An internal back-office view and a public storefront over the same catalogue model, where each side shows a different subset of the same data.
A Django REST Framework APIView that negotiates JSONRenderer and TemplateHTMLRenderer for the same resource, keeping content negotiation in one endpoint while each renderer owns its format.
A Qt Widgets application in which one QAbstractItemModel feeds table, list, or tree views so several presentations of the same document stay synchronized.
An ASP.NET Core Web API action whose JSON and XML output formatters select a response representation from the client's Accept header without changing the domain model.
avoid_when: Only one representation exists or is planned: a single Template View or Page Controller (one handler, one format) is simpler and has no negotiation indirection.

The 'other views' are really different consumers: when channels consume data rather than render it, expose one API and let each client render (Data Transfer Object plus a client-side presentation pattern) instead of adding server-side view technologies.
The representations must differ in data, not only in layout: that is a different projection or model, not one model with several views.

The framework already negotiates what you need (Spring's ContentNegotiatingViewResolver, Rails respond_to, ASP.NET Core output formatters, DRF renderers) - configure it rather than building a second view registry beside it.
The second view is a one-off script or a scheduled report: a direct export is cheaper than a permanent negotiated presentation layer.
The data is a single scalar or a trivial value with exactly one presentation.
anti_patterns: Serializing the domain entity into every format: internal fields and relations leak into the API or the export, and lazy-loaded collections fire per element.
A view-technology zoo: JSP plus Thymeleaf plus a PDF library plus a serializer 'just in case', each with its own template of the same screen - n templates and n test suites for one page.
Duplicated presentation logic: the same rounding, date format, permission filter and field selection reimplemented in the HTML template, the serializer and the export.
Rendering the same thing twice: the HTML view fetches its data with its own query while the API view loads the model again, doubling database work per request.
Negotiating on the URL suffix only while clients and caches speak Accept (or the reverse), so the same URL resolves to different representations under different proxies.
Hand-writing markup inside a serializer or JSON inside a template, bypassing each technology's escaping and creating an injection surface.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: presentation technology is a separate concern from the domain data and its rules (Separated Presentation).
Open/closed principle: new representations arrive through registration or configuration, not through edits to the model or to sibling views.
Single responsibility: one view per representation technology; choosing among them belongs to the resolver, not to the view.
DRY where it matters: share the model and the logical view, not the markup.
Information hiding: each view receives only the projection its representation needs, nothing 'just in case'.
Dependency inversion: views and negotiation depend on abstractions (renderer contract, projection), not on each other.
best_practices: Keep the model presentation-free and give the views a shared projection so that field selection and formatting rules exist exactly once.
Use per-representation DTOs or serializers instead of serializing entities; that is where 'what leaves the system' is decided.
Centralise negotiation: one resolver or format table, an explicit default, and 406 for unsupported representations instead of a silent fallback.
Prefer the framework's negotiation where it exists and keep only genuinely new technologies as custom views.
Test each representation against a fixed model and add one cross-representation consistency test for the fields that must agree across channels.
Cache the expensive representations rather than the model: HTML pages and exports are Page Cache candidates, the API payload usually is not.
Keep escaping with its technology (auto-escaped templates, serializer-escaped payloads) and never build markup by hand in a non-markup view.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2002), Chapter 14 'Web Presentation Patterns' - Model View Controller and the separated-presentation split that lets one model carry several independent views; MVC itself originates in Reenskaug's Smalltalk work of the late 1970s.

Krasner & Pope, 'A Cookbook for Using the Model-View-Controller User Interface Paradigm in Smalltalk-80', Journal of Object-Oriented Programming 1(3), 1988 - a model may have many view/controller pairs, each observing it independently.

Fowler, 'Organizing Presentation Logic' (further enterprise application patterns, 2006) - separating presentation logic from the view 'allows you to support multiple different views with the same logical behavior'.
Fowler, 'Presentation Domain Data Layering' (bliki, 2015) - 'This separation allows me to build multiple presentations on top of the same domain logic without duplicating it.'
